Private Members' Business
listening to me but he ought to seek more information. Supporting labour unions is fine, but so is promoting productivity.
I am pleased when people talk about car manufacturers because I happen to live next door to Sainte-Therese, as you know, and Windsor is not the only place where people can make cars. I listened to the NDP Member brag about talking to the labour unions and helping them, yet, Mr. Speaker, we know that their own candidate in Chambly, listen to this, it may be worth your while-
His own candidate in Chambly-and we know that the NDP is pro-union-named the Lada "car of the year" when he was with the APA, the Automobile Protection Association. Think of it: the Lada as car of the year! You should be ashamed to say that you represent the unions, because Lada is a Russian car made with Italian parts and as a driver I can tell you that there was no worse piece of junk!
Anyway, if members of the New Democratic Party encourage such things, they really have a nerve to talk about it in the House. I know about it because I was in the car business and close to the candidate who is running in Chambly. You always have to look at yourself in the mirror.
He then talked about the problem of the fisheries and he probably does not even know the real problem with the fisheries because I just spoke with the minister and it seems that it is not quite as he said.
He talked about Sainte-Therese. Certainly the government is proud that it can say today in the House that we supported the auto industry, whether in Sainte-Therese or in Bromont. We saved Sainte-Therese and with it, over 3,000 jobs. So I think that the government has fulfilled its responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the NDP often boasts of being more Catholic than the Pope, but sometimes I have serious doubts when they encourage sales of Ladas, which are not even made here. You could buy one for $6,000 and two weeks later, if you wanted to return it, it was worth only $400. I have serious questions. The candidate running in Chambly did that. The hon. member-the candidate in Chambly. He is not a member of Parliament and I hope he never will be. In any case, that is what you are doing, and it must be hard to convince people you are pro-union, when you urge people to buy
a car made in Russia that was a complete disaster. So let's be realistic!
Mr. Speaker, we are trying to improve our competitive position internationally by taking a specific approach that consists in: defending the needs of industry, as we have done, to ensure it is not overlooked when setting essential, macro-economic policies; conducting joint initiatives with industry to help it improve product quality and increase market share within a reasonable length of time, as we did with General Motors in Sainte-Therese; ensuring that government aid is compatible with our international obligations and treaties; providing increased aid and services for industry to promote development and dissemination of strategic technologies, market development and other innovation-oriented activities; providing less financial assistance for manufacturing facilities and more for research and development and technological development-as the hon. member said earlier, we need people with better training for certain industries.
These objectives and the focus of ISTC were established following close consultations in early 1988 with the provinces and representatives of national organizations as well as with people from the business, scientific and academic communities. These groups generally supported the mandate and direction of ISTC and helped us determine which initiatives should be a priority.
One of ISTC's major new initiatives has been to promote the development of strategic technologies that are essential to enhancing the competitive position of a wide range of industries, and I am referring to advanced industrial materials, biotechnology and information technology.
Today, the focus is on three main objectives: to support the creation of research and development alliances between business and universities in order to develop and disseminate new technologies; to support the creation of alliances focussing on technology applications in order to promote risk-sharing in connection with research and development projects and certain feasibility studies; and to promote technology management in a joint effort by ISTC, industry and universities.
Under the Technology Outreach Program, we are trying to improve productivity and competitiveness, especially in small businesses, by accelerating the acquisition,
January 23, 1990

development and dissemination of new technology and essential skills.
Mr. Speaker, I could also talk about advantageous initiatives and sector competitiveness, but I am running out of time.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to inform the House that two major objectives underlie all ISTC initiatives, and these are to defend the interests of business and the scientific community in cabinet, in areas such as taxation, transport and energy; to provide businesses with support and information to help them market their products and acquire new technology; and to increase competitiveness and adapt to the new business climate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to thank my hon. colleague from Windsor, Ontario for raising this motion in the House today. It is a timely and extremely important issue which deserves our attention and our action.
As we can see from the headlines in the daily newspapers, our world is changing. We are facing lay-offs in the forestry industry. In Bas-Caraquet the fish packing plant is closed. In Shippagan the plant is in receivership. In Canso, North Sydney, Lockeport, Wood Harbour, Port Medway, Port Mouton the plants are closed. Small towns across the country are boarding up windows and closing down.
Obviously we simply cannot rely on our fishery, our forests and our farms to provide jobs and wealth in this country. We are now emerging from a global round of competition which, by all reports, indicate that we must re-evaluate our economic and political priorities. In this highly competitive and creative world our traditional policies are just not good enough any longer. We have to alter our course.

The second half of this decade has been characterized by the restructuring, on a global scale, of companies trying to adjust to the new international environment.
Before setting our goals, we must know our roots. History shows that most firms base their economic and social policies on their national culture.
Private Members' Business
Ironically, Canada's problems derive from its strengths. Our natural resources have always provided us with a high standard of living. But, even though we cut down more trees than any other country, we are still importing chain saws. In 1987, the value of imported manufactured goods in Canada exceeded that of exported goods by $24 billion, which represents $460 million a week.
For example, we are importing 76 per cent of our machinery, 40 per cent of our electrical appliances and 80 per cent of our medical equipment.

Trade in advanced technology has grown almost twice as fast as trade in general. By 1995 trade in computers, aerospace equipment, electronic machinery and pharmaceuticals will account for one-quarter of total world exports. But Canada is largely missing out on this growing opportunity. For example, in 1980 our trade deficit in high-tech products totalled $4.6 billion. By 1987 this deficit increased to over $7 billion.
Recently we were told that Canada has experienced its first monthly merchandise trade deficit in thirteen and a half years. It is particularly noteworthy that this deficit included a sharp increase in imports of machinery and equipment during that month.
As the Premier of Ontario told the National Forum of Science and Technology Advisory Council this past June:
Increasingly, we are exporting yesterday's goods, and importing
tomorrow's technology.
We are currently putting 1.3 per cent of our Gross National Product into research and development. Our competitors are doing twice that much. For example, 7 per cent of Ontario manufacturing industries do not have even one engineer on staff. So what can they do but import products, technologies and the very knowledge needed to put them to use.
If we want to win in the international arena and thereby protect and enhance the quality of life of our citizens we must set our sights on competing with the very best. In an article published by The Globe and Mail last March Dr. Larkin Kerwin, President of the National Research Council wrote:

January 23, 1990
Private Members' Business
Canadians face some very unpleasant facts. Among the world's
industrial nations, we rank as technological illiterates; we have become
incompetents in the unfolding scientific civilization.
So what can we do about that? To start, we have to work together. Internationally speaking, Canada is simply too small to risk diluting its strength by each of us moving in different directions. We must work together and mobilize all of our sectors in a national effort. We must address this problem on a national scale.
This is not an issue which can be resolved in isolation of a federal, provincial or municipal government or by industry and labour alone. This is a problem which requires the collective effort by all elements of society. For example, in Ontario the government has brought together some of the finest minds from the world of business, labour, the academic community, and government and established a special council. This premiers' council was set up to develop an internationally competitive economy. Basically, its goal is to produce a game plan for building on existing strengths and creating new ones.
The council is working to restructure core industries and to invest in high gross and emerging industries. It is also addressing the need for investment in people through education and skill training. Sub-committees of the council hold public forums in schools, factories and union halls.
The concept for the council was borrowed from the Japanese who have a council which is chaired by the Japanese Prime Minister. Clearly, this is the kind of co-operative constructive action that we need on a national level. But there is something else we must consider.
New industries and new technology is vital but if we are to take full advantage of it we must have the skill, the entrepreneurial people to use it, transfer it, and ensure that it benefits all.
Along with government incentives to manufacturers and technology-based industry, we must work together to create a well educated and highly skilled workforce. All the incentives and all the investment in the world will be useless unless we have a workforce with the
ability to adapt and learn the constantly changing skills of the modem workplace.
Interestingly enough, the Southern Literacy Study estimates that as many as 5 million Canadians are functionally illiterate. Although it is very difficult to estimate the cost of illiteracy, a Woods Gordon study conducted for the Business Thsk Force on Literacy put the cost to Canadian business in the range of $4 billion per year due to lost productivity, increased training costs and industrial accidents. The estimated cost to Canadian society as a whole is as high as $10 billion per year.
The problem is getting worse. Increasing technological sophistication in the workplace and in society generally has raised the level of reading, writing, and number skills required to be functionally literate.
An article in The Globe and Mail this fall indicated that 50 per cent of factories use high technology. This is the technology that is necessary to lower costs and make these companies more competitive. The article also indicates that in 53 per cent of the plants, managers encountered problems trying to hire skilled people to work with the advanced technologies. Obviously, efforts to increase the proportion of our economy involved in the manufacturing industry will be for nothing unless we have prepared our workforce to perform these new tasks. It is therefore absolutely vital that any effort between the government, industry and trade unions to increase domestic productions in high technology sectors must also include a commitment to work together to combat illiteracy and to increase the skill level in our workforce. Therefore, there is no doubt that focusing on the high technology manufacturing sector will pay off richly in terms of jobs, trade balances and the economic well-being of Canadian communities.
For example, a recent consultant report indicates that the city of Kanata, known as "Silicone Valley North" will see huge growth in the next 10 years. In fact, they estimate that employment in the high technology sector which now employs 7,000 people in this city will quadruple by the turn of the century.
Around the world we are seeing a new spirit of co-operation between government, businesses and people. That same spirit must be represented here in
January 23, 1990

Canada amongst all the various sectors of our nation if we are to ensure that the step into the next century will be alongside the economic leaders in the world.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   INDUSTRY IMPORT-REPLACEMENT PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment as I begin. I believe the opportunity to speak during Private Members' Hour on Private Members' Bills and Motions is very important. I believe some of the most meaningful debate actually takes places here. I am pleased to have the opportunity and I thank my colleague for Essex-Windsor for introducing the motion today.
I suggest there is very little difference among people in all parties on many items when it comes to developing our industries, especially our high-tech and advance industries on which our future will depend. I think all members will agree that there should be more R & D. There should be more development and co-operation with industry, with the universities, with unions and with all parties that can work together to forge success in this area.
However, there may be many differences as to the approaches we take to achieve those priorities. I would like to refer to one example that was used by the Member for Essex-Windsor. It is one that is near and dear to my heart. When it comes to the forest industry in Canada no one in the world can produce lumber like we can. When it comes to the technology surrounding it, although we have many of the fresh ideas and new thoughts, the blooms of this new technology, we really have not been as successful in the development of that industry.
I would concur that that is an area in which we should be working with the universities for their R & D, and with small business and large business to try to encourage that development. It is extremely important that this business, when developed, is good sound business that can survive.
The member for member from Essex-Windsor gave us the example of pulp and paper equipment as something that we should be developing ourselves. I would be the first to say "Good. Let's get at it." Let us see if we can be competitive.
It would not be very realistic to think that we could develop equipment strictly for the use of Canadians. If we develop something in pulp and paper technology it has to have a wider economic base than just Canada and
Private Members' Business
would obviously have to be successful world-wide. We cannot just close our border for our own use of all the pulp and paper equipment or all electric motors that we use.
In order to develop this new technology, our priority should be to focus on international competitiveness. That is one way we can make that development work.
Any effort by Canada in the past to look inwards has not worked. Import replacement policies, as it is referred to, involves a number of practices that do not sit well with the economic realities of today's competitive world, nor do they accord well with the views of the present government on how best to achieve sustained economic growth.
In the past some industries were often selected by the government of the day as having growth potential. They were then given support and this support usually meant putting up trade barriers or non tariff barriers for the import of goods from other countries in the hope that the essential ingredients for sustained commercial success would be achieved by these industries.
These so-called infant industries were supposed to grow big and strong and stand on their own feet. In many cases, this did not happen. Those infant industries just did not grow up. The end result was that we were forcing on our own economy higher prices and inefficiency. It is that type of inward looking growth that we must try to avoid.
These approaches were inappropriate for the 1950s, 1960s, and even the 1970s. In some instances they led to the establishment in Canada of successful industries, but very few. In a world now that requires intense competition and rapid change, that is not the direction in which I feel we should be going.
One of the keys on which we have to focus in Canada if we are going to achieve that success, and one on which this government has been focusing, is the program of excellence, whether it be in industry, in our universities or in small business.
We must be able to produce and supply what the markets demand and, most important, at the right price. We must be competitive. This requires the right combination of up-to-date technology, the right mix of inputs, good delivery and servicing, flexibility and just plain old fashioned good management. We cannot hope to do everything well. We must find a niche in which we can

January 23, 1990
Private Members' Business
succeed, where we can take competitive advantages and build on it until we are successful.
Another area to which the government is giving greater consideration is the removal of some our interior barriers. It is not enough to take down the barrier in trading between here and the United States because in many cases inter-provincial trade is very limited. We should be addressing that question and I am glad to say that the provinces and the federal government are co-operating in this area.
I am proud to be a part of this government which I believe is taking some very commendable steps through the Department of Industry, Science and Technology for initiatives that will go a long way toward achieving many of the successes that we have been talking about here today.
There is much more I would like to say on this topic but the time is short. In conclusion, it is obvious that the aim of the government is to create in Canada a program of excellence for industry on a world class science and technology base. The government has renewed and strengthened this commitment to R and D and to co-operative efforts with industry. It is the task of this new department to translate this commitment into action.
The key today is global trading. In Canada especially, we know that we can succeed, but there is a real risk of failing if we look too much inward. There are prime examples of this around the world. China has been an inward looking economy and government, surrounded by smaller, but so much more successful centres of economic excellence. Singapore, Taiwan, Hong Kong, these are all peoples of the same nationality with great success because they look to the world for their market.
There is a similar example we see in Europe, with East Germany and West Germany. One is looking inward and the other is looking to the world markets, building on their successes, building their technological excellence. Why.should we in Canada do anything different?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   INDUSTRY IMPORT-REPLACEMENT PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my thoughts to those of my colleagues, especially the member from Cariboo-Chil-cotin who gave an excellent speech. I would like to add my thoughts on the motion put forward by my hon.
colleague the member for Essex-Windsor, who proposes that the government develop measures to increase import replacement production in Canada.
Import replacement is a somewhat archaic concept, since it takes us back to the notion of small, inefficient industries protected by high tariff walls. In today's global economy, a company cannot rely on servicing only a small captive market. Successive trade liberalization efforts under GATT have progressively lowered the tariffs since the end of World War II.
Combined with the increasing output of newly industrialized countries, it means that our industries are facing increasing competition at home and abroad and are themselves challenging others in an international marketplace. Given the dependence of our economy on international trade, inward looking protectionist measures are not the road to survival and success. The key is to enhance the competitiveness of Canadian industry.
At the time of the Depression tariff walls were 80 per cent higher than they are today. As we have lowered them, Canada has become increasingly competitive and we should only seek to do more of this in the future.
It was in this spirit that the Prime Minister announced in August, 1987, the creation of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology and charged it with the mandate of building up Canadian industry's international competitiveness with all sectors and with both overseas and home markets in mind.
We need world-class industries to create and maintain a world-class economy. Import replacement is not a viable development strategy. Canadian companies must develop innovative technologies and products and achieve sufficient scale in production to address the world market. Only then can they sustain the continuous reinvestment that is required to generate future generations of products. The Canadian market is simply not big enough.
For example, Canada is a world leader in telecommunications. TTiis industry is the engine that drives all our high technology sectors. With global sales of over $8 billion, it employs over 150,000 highly skilled, knowledgeable workers. Our world strength in telecommunications has come about because of a coincidence of geography and government policy. Our country is so vast, the communication challenge is so great that we had to become world leaders. We had to break new ground.
January 23, 1990

Today this industry is responding to the challenges offered to it by nations all around the world.
The rapidly growing companies that make up this industry must expand into new global markets to ensure their future. More generally, ISTC consultations with industry have pointed out that unless we respond quickly as a nation to build on our successes and develop our comparative advantage in areas like information technologies, we will be rapidly surpassed by the newly industrialized nations like Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and the others that my colleague from Cariboo-Chilcotin mentioned.
These countries are making investments necessary to emerge as the tigers of the 21st century. As they make these investments and as their economies grow, wages increase and the standard of living increases. It has increased rapidly. Many of these countries are what I would call economic miracles.
The appropriate role for government is to encourage Canadian industry to become and remain competitive. For example, through establishing appropriate macroeconomic and other policies, disseminating information on changing domestic and international circumstances and market opportunities, and providing specific services where needed. We must examine new ways of doing business. We must explore new options.
One of the most important advantages that any Canadian manufacturer in whatever sector, for example, machinery or textiles, has over a foreign competitor is time. What every customer seeks is the right product at the right place and perhaps more importantly at the right time. This is why officials at ISTC are spending considerable effort to encourage Canadian industry to put in place and use more efficient and speedy communication linkages between raw material suppliers, equipment suppliers, manufacturers, retailers and consumers. Such linkages are facilitated through encouragement and support to industry associations and councils.
Through sector competitiveness initiatives, ISTC works with selected industry sectors as well as other government departments and agencies to identify constraints and opportunities, define industry-wide needs and put together in co-operation with industry a fully
Private Members' Business
integrated and complementary action plan to realize these opportunities. This comprehensive approach will help to ensure the future strength of those industries in the market-place.
Another positive, forward-looking initiative to which the government has devoted a lot of time and energy is that of encouraging the development of Canadian suppliers, particularly small business, to the federal government. In collaboration with the Departments of Supply and Services, Transport and National Defence, Industry Science and Technology has worked on the source development program. Source development is a concept designed to provide industry with historical market information on federal purchases, particularly by National Defence and Transport, Transport currently contracting outside of Canada or having low over-all Canadian content.
This is particularly important to us in western Canada where historically the federal government has purchased few products. This is gradually and slowly working. We are optimistic that it will continue.
Tax reform, strengthening international partnerships, deficit control through spending restraint, and good management all contribute to the government objectives of building a strong and fully competitive economy. Innovative and forward-looking industrial strategies are also essential. That is why the ISTC is working with industry and universities to bring about a greater and more effective integration of our scientific, technological and industrial activities to improve commercial competitiveness.
In conclusion, it is not by imposing trade barriers but by improving our competitive strength on a continual basis that we can effectively forestall excessive import penetration. Indeed, increased imports are not a cause for concern if they are a reflection of increased rationalization and specialization by Canadian producers on fewer but highly competitive products which are successfully exported.
Such trends are evident in a number of areas. In some sectors of machinery, aerospace and other industries, while imports are still substantial our exports in these

January 23, 1990
Adjournment Debate
sectors in niche products and niche markets have been improving significantly for over two decades.
These challenges and choices we face as a nation can best be addressed by outward looking policies focused on being internationally competitive rather than by backward and inward looking protectionist policies.

Mr. Speaker, on December 5,1 stood in the House to ask the government to explain its agricultural program cuts in light of the negotiations that are ongoing with regard to subsidies in the GATT round of negotiations.
I posed this question in part because a few days before, on the weekend, the Minister for Grains and Oilseeds had been speaking to the Alberta Wheat Pool in Calgary and he was quoted as saying in the Calgary Herald of Saturday, December 2, that he was assuring the Pool delegates that Canada is not about to make changes to its agricultural subsidy programs during the current round of international trade negotiations without similar moves by other nations. He was quoted as saying that we have no intention of getting into a situation where we give up some of our support unless other countries are doing the same thing.
It was very hard to understand how the minister could say that with a straight face after having been in the negotiations for three or four years. During that time, Canada has given up the two-price wheat system. We have given up interest free cash advances to farmers. We have virtually given up tax rebates for farm fuel to farmers. They have been cut another 65 per cent as of January 1 of this year. We knew the cut was coming when I asked the question.
Research funds have been cut or frozen, meaning that there are less funds to do the same amount of work next year because of the inflation that exists in research. Crop insurance funding carried by the federal government
dropped from 45 per cent of the total cost to something like 25 per cent of the total cost.
There are probably even more programs that I could have listed in Question Period at the time. It is obvious that the government is not following the policy that the minister outlined in Calgary. I wanted to get some of the ministers to explain why they were, in fact, giving up what the U.S. considers to be subsidies under their producer subsidy equivalent program that they are touting in these international talks when none of the other countries are.
We gave up interest free cash advances while the Americans continue their advance program. We have given up our two-price wheat program which had the effect in low markets of paying the farmer more money for his wheat that was to be consumed domestically while the Americans continue a massive subsidy program to their farmers.
Since that time, the Americans have also continued and stepped up their export enhancement program, a program that raised the ire of this House on all sides when they began paying from $7 to $12 a tonne to customers to take their grain from them. They are now up to $20.95 a tonne on the last major sales to China and U.S.S.R.
The U.S. continues to increase its aid to farmers with the money it is pouring into agriculture, while this government responds by reducing the amount of aid, even though the talks are ongoing. This concerns me, my party, and farmers as well because when this kind of negotiation is going on, ultimately at the end of the round all sides are asked to lay their cards on the table, so to speak, and name which programs they are going to cut. While there is a clause at the beginning of this round that says that cuts made during the program should count at the end of the day, they really do not. In all previous negotiations what normally counts is what is put on the table at that particular time and that is what the Americans and Europeans will demand again this time.
In my supplementary question I raised concerns about how these program cuts were harming existing programs and I referred to a copy of a memo that I had received from the agriculture research branch, namely, the Animal Research Centre, whereby the director notifies all staff as follows:
January 23, 1990

We have now put together a clearer picture of the Animal Research Centre's financial situation. As a result, I must advise you that there can be no further purchases of supplies or services from now until March 31, 1990. This includes travel, rentals, stock from B.R.C. stores, etc.
Steps have been taken to ensure that our livestock and poultry will have all basic requirements met. We are currently reviewing all avenues to determine whether any research activities can be continued. However, until further notice, no expenditures will be approved.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, we have this great research centre sitting there unable to conduct any research and concerned that it may not even be able to feed the animals that it has.
I did not get any response from the Minister of State for Agriculture on that issue and I would hope that today the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture will be able to shed some light on these cuts and tiy to justify why his government persists in cutting back funding to agriculture and reducing the research impact that the department has.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government certainly has supported the needs of the Canadian agri-food industry and it has never wavered here at home or internationally.
The hon. member for Mackenzie is taking us to task for adjustments that have been made to our agricultural programs over the last year. Of course we have had to make adjustments; the changes taking place in agriculture demand it. And I can assure the hon. member that we will continue to respond to the changing agriculture environment. These adjustments to our policies and programs have been consistent with the objectives outlined in the national agriculture strategy signed by federal and provincial agriculture ministers in 1986. They are consistent with the national policy review we are currently leading.
The hon. member has suggested that our agriculture policy is authored by our international trading partners and that they are GATT driven. This is simply not the case. The government has and will continue to develop agriculture policy that meets Canadians' needs and conditions.
Yes, we have adjusted our programs in a way that also reflects our goal and approach in the MTN. This does
Adjournment Debate
not mean we have softened in the defence of our agri-food industry. We firmly maintain our right to design programs that suit Canadians' needs but are also consistent with our international obligations.
That is why Canada is working hard with other countries for international trade reform through multilateral trade negotiations. We expect all countries will agree to adjust their policies consistent with the new rules that are being negotiated. This will reduce trade distortions and lead to a fairer and more open international trading system.
I also want to assure the hon. member that this government remains committed to agriculture research in Canada. Agriculture Canada is a leader in this area with an annual research budget of $250 million. We will continue to support this activity to meet the needs of the agri-food industry.
In fact, research at our Central Experimental Farm here in Ottawa is being enhanced and refocused to reflect industry concerns. This is also happening at the Animal Research Centre in Ottawa because industry has picked up long-term animal breeding technology developed at the centre. The arc is now moving toward the development of new technology to improve animal production. The centre is reorienting its research programs toward the key areas of safety and quality of food, animal bio-technology, animal behaviour and environmental quality. However, the centre is moving in these scientific directions at the same time as existing programs are being completed. Because of this, the centre was heading toward a serious budget overrun in this transition period and extra controls had to be imposed.
Funding to the centre has not been cut and frozen, as the hon. member has stated. Rather, expenditures are being managed and controlled within the existing budget for the remainder of the fiscal year. This is not only ensuring that the centre can continue to provide essential services but also that it has this flexibility to meet urgent needs and maintain ongoing research programs. We are trying to do the maximum research with the resources available.
This government is committed to providing the sort of agricultural policies and programs that are in tune with the needs of our agri-food industry and we will continue to adjust these policies and our programs.

January 23, 1990
Adjournment Debate EMERGENCY MEASURES

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today during today's adjournment debate to speak on an issue which is of great importance.
On October 18 of last year, one day after the devastating San Francisco earthquake, I rose in the House to ask the Minister of National Defence about the government's lack of support for programs relating to emergency preparedness. The Minister of National Defence is the lead minister responsible for emergency preparedness and I regret to say that I was less than satisfied with his response. I appreciate the opportunity to further discuss this issue as several months have now passed. I would hate to think that the government has forgotten this whole issue.
As the House knows, this government made severe cuts to the earthquake prediction research program of Energy, Mines and Resources. It is indeed unfortunate as Canada is susceptible to earthquakes. Near Newfoundland, Yukon and Baffin Islands, high risk zones exist. As well, Vancouver Island and the lower mainland of British Columbia, where my riding is, are also at high risk. There is a high population density in these latter regions. If a serious earthquake should occur, and experts agree it is just a matter of time, the damage to property and the loss of life will be stupendous.
Last October, we saw the graphic and heart-wrenching images from the San Francisco earthquake. We were all relieved to know that the death toll was not as high as it might have been. It was thanks to improved preparedness that the city of San Francisco was able to cope. Would the people of southwest British Columbia be as fortunate?
Let us look at the reality of the situation. Each year Japan spends $100 per person on earthquake preparedness. San Francisco alone spends $19 per person. In Canada, we spend 29 cents.
Our Constitution outlines disaster response as multifaceted. Municipalities are the first to respond in a disaster. As they are financially unable to carry this out, they must turn for funding to the provinces who must turn to the federal government for financial assistance. This is not an alien concept. The federal government has had the revenue raising system in place designed to pass
along needed funds to the provinces and to the municipalities.
This issue is of great importance in the lower mainland of British Columbia. Experts say two possibilities face this region: a major quake of up to 7.5 on the Richter scale will occur every 30 to 50 years or a catastrophe quake of more than 8 will occur every 500 years.
I am concerned about this because I believe we face several risks. Many Vancouver area highrises were built before 1975's building codes came into effect. Vancouver's airport is only three metres above sea level and the earth under its runways could liquefy, rendering the airport useless. Two major dams, the Cleveland and the Seymour Falls dams, need further investigation into their ability to withstand a quake.
Last fall in the Vancouver area, thousands of parents were alarmed to find their children were attending schools which would likely collapse in the event of an earthquake. If we happen to get an earthquake which measures 8, a catastrophe, cities would be devastated and comprehensive damage would occur from Seattle right to Prince Rupert. Experts in B.C. have repeatedly stated that emergency planning is hampered by a lack of support by the federal and the provincial governments. The Greater Vancouver Regional District has told the province that a hazard analysis needs to be done on the major lifeline systems, hospitals, roads, bridges and pipelines. The province has yet to fund this.
Furthermore, the province has suggested that after a major earthquake we would have to wait 24 hours before the province would provide assistance. I do not know what the provincial government believes, but if it thinks that the injured and the dying could put everything on hold for 24 hours before needing support, it better think again.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, let me make one point perfectly clear. Experts have said time and time again that southwestern British Columbia is a high risk earthquake zone. They have said that the loss of life would be extremely high should a massive earthquake occur. They have also said the best way to prevent such a tragedy is to prepare for an earthquake.
We all know the most important first step in preparedness is prediction. Why, then, Mr. Speaker, did this government cut back the earthquake prediction pro-
January 23, 1990

gram? Why has the government jeopardized the entire earthquake preparedness program by attacking its very foundation?
I would like to remind the minister of what he said in this House on October 18, as found in Hansard at page 4810. In commenting on the role of the federal government to the two other levels of government he said:
We co-operate with them as a national government. We provide the
expertise that we can provide.
I think it is past time that the minister acted on his own words. It is time to co-operate. It is time to provide that much needed expertise. The minister has a choice in this matter. He can restore funding to the prediction program, thereby enabling scientists and the Emergency Measures Organization to have fair warning of earthquakes, or we can all wake up one morning to find that an earthquake has devastated British Columbia and perhaps killed hundreds and destroyed millions of dollars worth of property.
The choice, Mr. Speaker, is the choice of this government. It is the choice of the minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should have directed her question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp), since seismic research is his department's responsibility. However, as parliamentary secretary to the Minister responsible for emergency preparedness, I am quite interested in the issue of earthquake prediction. For this reason, I tried to find out the reason why budgetary cuts were made in that area. It is simply this: Budget cuts were made in this particular program as part of the effort the government is making to curtail federal program spending generally, as recommended by the Nielsen Task Force. It was simply a matter of budgetary priorities.
This year, the credits allocated to the Earthquake Prediction Research Program were increased by $400,000. They will provide better means to monitor earthquakes in Canada as a whole and in Vancouver Island in particular and to seek evidence of earth's crust tension associated with earthquakes. They will help also develop new seismic hasard analysis methods and deter-
Adjoumment Debate
mine their degree of reliability for the purpose of updating our building standards.
Mr. Speaker, I must remind you that the federal government has initiated a serious disaster response planning to meet the needs of all Canadian provinces and territories in case of earthquakes, for it is first and foremost a provincial and territorial responsibility.
In reply more specifically to my honourable colleague who claimed just now that it was strictly to send money, I just cannot understand why the federal government is always being asked for new funds to carry out provincial responsibilities when the provinces and municipalities have just as much taxation powers as the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for allowing me to come back and re-ask a question that I asked in this House in October of 1989. The question was with respect to VIA Rail and the announcement made by the Minister of Transport in that time period when he told us that the business plan called for the elimination of certain routes in this country and that the transcontinental train service, VIA passenger train which travels from coast to coast in Canada, was going to be reduced to three days a week from seven days a week. For the train to get from the east to the west, it must go through northern Ontario from Sudbury or Capreol through to the Manitoba border.
In that area of our country and part of the riding I represent, there are two rail lines what are commonly referred to as the northern line and the southern line, which follows Lake Superior. They are known to be competitive in scenic beauty with the trip from Calgary to Vancouver through the Rocky Mountains. I was on the last train as it went through this beautiful area of the country. Having been on both those lines, it is hard to imagine that this government would make that move to eliminate the southern route through northern Ontario.
It defies logic in as much as the line that was chosen to continue the transcontinental train across Canada is a line that only services 14,000 people in its northern route as against in excess of 256,000 people through the

January 23, 1990
Adjournment Debate
southern route of northern Ontario. The figures are based on actual accounts of Statistics Canada, using the 1986 census.
The reality of the matter is simply this. In the VIA cuts that were announced on that date by the minister, cuts which have met with so much opposition from coast to coast, there are many areas that have to and will experience from January 15 onwards a very reduced service of passenger rail service. The reality that we face in northern Ontario is the fact that we do not have a reduced service. As of January 15, 1990, we no longer have passenger rail service through northern Ontario in the communities of Marathon, Terrace Bay, Shreiber, Nipigon, Red Rock, Kirkit, Dorion, Thunder Bay, Ig-nace, Dryden and Kenora as it goes up into Winnipeg.
These areas just mentioned enjoyed passenger rail service in this country for over 100 years. It is doubly difficult to accept that move by the government because in this particular area we do not have the infrastructure that many other areas of our country have with respect to roads. Some of the communities that I mentioned have alternate bus service or adequate roads or airport terminals.
The very logical question I asked the minister is how he could make that decision. The response I received was that in the decision, we considered it was better at the time to keep the service for what is called the remote communities rather than for Thunder Bay and Sudbury which have better modes of transportation.
After making those statements, I invite the minister to visit Thunder Bay and Sudbury. Perhaps he would like to tell the people directly that he figures it would be better to provide a service where there are no people than to provide a service in Sudbury where there are approximately 125,000 people and also in Thunder Bay where there are 125,000 people.
I do not question that there may be some remote areas in Canada which do not have access to other modes of transportation. However, I assured the minister on that date and subsequent to that that the line he cut, the line from Sudbury or Capreol through to Thunder Bay and on into Winnipeg was not a remote route any longer, nor did it test on all the communities on that route, nor did it pass the test of remoteness.
What is the critical test of remoteness? It is whether any of these communities have any other means of transportation. I showed in explicit form, based on the
statistics already mentioned that the communities, although perhaps remote at one time, within the 12 years since VIA has existed, were now accessible by a fair quality of highway. They were accessible by bus or a combination of bus-highway or an adequate airport. So the test of remoteness did not apply in this particular area from Capreol or Sudbury through the southern route to Thunder Bay, Ignace, Dryden, Kenora and on to Winnipeg.
Both of those arguments were not only made in this House, they were made in committee and in personal meetings with the Minister of Transport and in personal meetings when the mayors and reeves of all of these communities in northern Ontario came to Ottawa to meet with the minister to see if they could get a change of mind.
The minister responded to my supplementary question by saying that it has been a scenario we have used for the whole country. We have people in this country who do not have any other mode of transportation. As I have said, I do not disagree with this. What I object to is the government labelling the CN line as remote when it is actually not, and it does not present a factual, logical conclusion to the argument I have just made.
I see that my time is running short. Let me just rephrase the question for my hon. friend. I appreciate him being here to reply.
It still does not make any logical sense that the northern route through northern Ontario was chosen rather than the southern route. If he can explain to me, through you, Mr. Speaker, why it is better and more economical to service 14,000 people rather than to service 256,000 people with passenger rail service in this country, I would like to hear his answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take the opportunity to respond to the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon about his question on the selection of which northern route to take in the reorganization of VIA's transcontinental service.
I am sure that in the next few minutes, I will not convince the hon. member that they have made the right selection, because he obviously has a bias in this. He comes from Thunder Bay-Nipigon, and that is one area not represented by VIA to the fullest extent that it has been in times past.
January 23, 1990

As part of the government's announcement of a national, affordable and sustainable network, the minister indicated that VIA would continue to provide service to truly isolated communities with no alternative means of transportation.
Back in October when the hon. member raised his question, he said that the communities from Sudbury to Chapleau, White River, Marathon, Nipigon, Thunder Bay, Dryden, Kenora and on to Winnipeg will lose their rail service link along CP's line in northern Ontario. In making that statement, I think he was playing around a little bit with his geography. He knows the area well, far better that I do. But in making his statement, the hon. member has overlooked the fact that VIA's Sudbuiy-White River service on the CP rail line continues in place under the government's decision.
It may be that the hon. member has overlooked these communities in making his statement. I can assure him that they were not overlooked when the decision was being made about what lines would have to be cut in order to fit within the framework of the money that we wish to expend in the subsidies to VIA Rail.
Similarly, the truly remote communities of the Winni-peg-Capreol portion of CN's line will be covered by operations of VIA's new restructured transcontinental
Adjournment Debate
service. For the communities between White River, Thunder Bay and Winnipeg, my information is that the total population of that particular area is only about 150,000 and not 350,000. We will have to sit down together and go through these numbers.
We also know that these communities are all served by the Trans-Canada Highway and all have high frequency bus service. In conclusion, the choice of routes reflects the government's intention to strike a balance between the transportation needs of Canada and the fiscal realities. The government's decision is not only financially responsible, but it meets the needs for a sustainable, national network.
I can also say in all truthfulness that the decisions were very, very difficult to make when it was decided what would be kept and what would be dropped. There is no way that you can satisfy all of the needs and what people would like to have through the rail passenger service.
